prompt: A bicycle shop plans its content calendar. Name the funnel stage each piece serves.

cases.text: An original survey of 2,000 city commuters on how long their trips to work take by car, bus and bike.
cases.explanation: Original research attracts people exploring a problem, not yet a brand.

cases.text: A five-question quiz that recommends a frame type for the rider's terrain and budget.
cases.explanation: An interactive product finder helps shoppers narrow their consideration set.

cases.text: A height and inseam calculator beside the add-to-cart button that names the right frame size.
cases.explanation: A sizing calculator resolves final purchase hesitation.

cases.text: A short page explaining that unridden bikes can be returned free within 30 days.
cases.explanation: A return-policy explainer reduces risk at the point of purchase.

cases.text: A monthly chain-cleaning checklist emailed to people who bought a bike.
cases.explanation: Maintenance checklists help owners get full value from the product.

cases.text: A side-by-side table of three e-bikes' range, weight and motor torque.
cases.explanation: A specification comparison matrix supports evaluation.

prompt: A furniture retailer is deciding which system should handle each job. Sort each job into the CRM or the CDP.

cards.text: Logging a customer's complaint about a scratched table and the replies the support team sent.
cards.explanation: Support tickets and communication history with known customers live in the CRM.

cards.text: Tracking a hotel chain's bulk order for 300 chairs through quote, negotiation and signature.
cards.explanation: Sales pipelines are a core CRM function.

cards.text: Ingesting two million anonymous product-page views per hour from the website and app.
cards.explanation: Real-time anonymous clickstreams are what a CDP is built to ingest.

cards.text: Joining an anonymous visitor's sofa views to her existing profile when she types her email at checkout.
cards.explanation: The CDP resolves identity when an anonymous visitor identifies herself.

cards.text: Sending a segment of recent lamp browsers to the ad network and the email platform every hour.
cards.explanation: A CDP syncs audience segments outward to other systems.

cards.text: Storing the phone number and delivery address of a customer who ordered by phone.
cards.explanation: Contact records of known customers are CRM data.

prompt: An online tea shop has set up its automated flows. Name the flow each message belongs to.

cases.text: The day the parcel arrives, a short guide on water temperature and steeping time for the green tea inside.
cases.explanation: Delivery triggers care instructions before the product is used.

cases.text: Minutes after someone joins the newsletter, an email on how the founder sources tea from three family farms, with the five best sellers.
cases.explanation: Subscribing triggers the brand story and best sellers.

cases.text: Twenty-six days after a customer bought a 30-day pouch of breakfast tea, a one-click reorder link.
cases.explanation: The message is timed just before the predicted run-out date.

cases.text: A logged-in shopper puts a tin of oolong in the cart and leaves, and three hours later gets a reminder that only four tins are left.
cases.explanation: An unfinished checkout triggers a timely reminder with stock status.

cases.text: A customer who used to order every six weeks has not ordered in five months and receives a 15 percent offer.
cases.explanation: Exceeding the expected inter-purchase window triggers a targeted incentive.

cases.text: Three weeks after a first order of loose-leaf tea, a suggestion for a glass teapot with a built-in strainer.
cases.explanation: Complementary recommendations after the item has been used are cross-sell.

question_text: An outdoor-gear store reviews one customer: she ordered nine times in the previous two years and spent 2,400 dollars in total, but her last order was eleven months ago. Which segment and treatment fit her best?
hint: Read each of R, F and M separately before naming the segment.
correct_answer_citation: Grouping customers into RFM segments (such as Champions with high R, F, and M, At-Risk Big Spenders with low R but high historical F and M, and Price-Sensitive One-Timers) allows marketers to reserve VIP early access for Champions while directing win-back interventions to At-Risk high-value buyers.

options.option_text: Champion, so she should get VIP early access to the new collection.
options.option_explanation: Her frequency and spend are high, but eleven months without an order means recency is low.

options.option_text: Price-Sensitive One-Timer, so she should get only the general newsletter.
options.option_explanation: Nine orders and 2,400 dollars rule out a one-time, low-value buyer.

options.option_text: At-Risk Big Spender, so she should get a targeted win-back intervention.
options.option_explanation: Correct. Low recency with high historical frequency and monetary value is the at-risk, high-value profile.

options.option_text: No segment can be assigned until she orders again, because recency is unknown.
options.option_explanation: Recency is known: it is the eleven months since her last purchase.

prompt: A running-shoe store's language model drafts follow-up emails. Sort each line by whether it stays useful or crosses into perceived surveillance.

cards.text: "Shoes with extra cushioning for long road runs", sent to a buyer who filters for cushioned shoes.
cards.explanation: It highlights the attribute the customer said she cares about.

cards.text: "Your 6 a.m. route along the river looked tough this morning", based on location data from the store's app.
cards.explanation: It reveals tracking the customer did not knowingly share.

cards.text: "Your size 9 in the trail model is back in stock", after the shopper signed up for a restock alert.
cards.explanation: The customer asked for this alert, so the detail is expected.

cards.text: "You looked at the red racing flats for 47 seconds on Tuesday at 10:18 p.m."
cards.explanation: An exact viewing time and duration signals granular behavioral tracking.

cards.text: "Is your knee still hurting?", inferred from searches for knee braces on the store's site.
cards.explanation: Inferring a health condition from browsing feels like surveillance.

cards.text: "Our lightest racing shoe, 180 grams", for a buyer whose past orders are all lightweight models.
cards.explanation: Attribute framing based on visible purchase history stays within expectations.
